purpose: Documents full-text editorial review of newly downloaded posts before canonical ingestion.

newKeywords: The Unknown Life of Jesus Christ

posts.title: Advice About Money From a Different Universe
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Argues that Jesus' advice about wealth requires reinterpretation because modern capitalism differs fundamentally from the agrarian economy underlying his teachings.
posts.searchSummary: Explains Jesus' demand to give wealth to the poor against the finite resources and widespread subsistence poverty of the ancient agrarian economy. Contrasts this setting with modern capitalism's capacity to generate additional wealth, while acknowledging its severe inequalities and harms. Argues that applying Jesus' economic teachings today requires historical reinterpretation rather than literal adoption of advice shaped by a different economic system.

posts.title: Outdated Religion and Modern Life
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Argues that Jesus' expectation of imminent judgment explains his demand to abandon wealth, while generosity remains relevant without that expectation.
posts.searchSummary: Connects Jesus' instruction to sell everything and help the poor with his conviction that divine judgment and God's kingdom were imminent. Explains why complete divestment no longer makes practical sense for people expecting society to continue, since resources sustain both ordinary life and future assistance. Distinguishes Jesus' literal apocalyptic demand from the enduring commitment to generosity and concern for those in need.

posts.title: Changing Times and the Question of Relevance
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Explores how changing historical circumstances affect the relevance of Jesus' radical teachings about giving up possessions and caring for others.
posts.searchSummary: Uses reflection on limited remaining time to introduce the relationship between expectations about the future and ethical priorities. Explains that Jesus urged individuals to abandon possessions and serve the needy within a religious and agrarian world unlike our own, rather than proposing economic reform. Argues that ancient advice cannot simply be transferred unchanged, while leaving open how its underlying purpose can guide modern behavior.

posts.title: Expecting the End? Was Mark Written in Aramaic? And Was a Key Verse Added to John?
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Compares modern Adventist expectations with Jesus' apocalyptic message, defends Mark's Greek composition, and explains why John 16:15 is probably original.
posts.searchSummary: Addresses three reader questions about modern apocalyptic beliefs, the language of Mark, and the originality of John 16:15. Traces Seventh-day Adventism to the failed prediction of 1844 and explains why Mark's style and occasional Aramaic expressions do not establish an Aramaic original. Attributes the missing Johannine verse in early witnesses to accidental copying errors caused by identical line endings, supported by its otherwise extensive manuscript attestation.

posts.title: The (Ir)relevance of Biblical Moral Teachings
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Argues that biblical moral teachings require historical interpretation before modern application, especially Jesus' command to relinquish possessions and help the poor.
posts.searchSummary: Examines biblical rules about slavery, family life, agriculture, and women's behavior in church to show how moral instructions depend on historical circumstances. Extends this problem to Jesus' demand that followers sell their possessions and give to the poor. Argues that responsible application requires identifying why an instruction made sense originally, how circumstances have changed, and whether its underlying ethical purpose remains useful today.

posts.title: A Modern Scholar Who Also Argues Jesus Did Not Die on the Cross
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Rejects Hugh Schonfield's reconstruction of a staged death and failed resurrection plot as historically unsupported, while distinguishing it from literary forgery.
posts.searchSummary: Critiques The Passover Plot, which portrays Jesus as arranging a drug-induced apparent death to fulfill messianic expectations before an unexpected spear wound ruins the plan. Contrasts this reconstruction with modern fabricated gospels that reshape Jesus to suit particular agendas. Stresses that Schonfield wrote under his own name as a historian, so the work is not a forgery, although its central historical premise is rejected.

posts.title: Did Jesus Survive His Crucifixion?  Depends Which Gospel You Read….
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Exposes a modern forged eyewitness account claiming Jesus survived crucifixion, using historical anachronisms and its dependence on earlier historical fiction.
posts.searchSummary: Examines The Crucifixion of Jesus, by an Eye-Witness, a purported ancient Essene letter claiming that Jesus survived the cross through secret healing and died months later. Identifies problems with its Latin language, references to later Gospels, and inaccurate portrayal of the Essenes. Explains Martin Dibelius's demonstration that the narrative was adapted from K. H. Venturini's modern historical fiction rather than preserved from an ancient witness.

posts.title: Ghosts in the Bible?  Check Out This New Blog by Travis Proctor
posts.author: Travis W. Proctor
posts.description: Interprets God's behavior in Eden through ancient Near Eastern portrayals of imperfect deities, challenging later assumptions about divine perfection and omniscience.
posts.searchSummary: Introduces Travis Proctor's Haunted Bible project through a guest essay on God's humanlike behavior in Genesis 2-3. Reads the creation of humans as laborers, God's questions, and the expulsion from Eden alongside Mesopotamian stories of self-interested and fallible gods. Argues that the narrative's apparent divine deception and limited knowledge make sense in their ancient setting rather than through later expectations of a perfect, omniscient deity.
topics: Divine Beings in the Hebrew Bible

posts.title: Did Jesus Go to India and Tibet?
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Traces claims that Jesus studied in India and Tibet to Nicolas Notovitch's forged account and explains how investigators exposed it.
posts.searchSummary: Recounts Nicolas Notovitch's claim to have obtained a Tibetan account of Jesus' lost years at Hemis monastery, published as The Unknown Life of Jesus Christ. Summarizes its story of Jesus studying Eastern religions before returning to Palestine. Describes scholarly objections and direct inquiries at the monastery that contradicted both the discovery story and the existence of the alleged manuscript, identifying the account as a modern hoax.
secondaryKeywords: The Unknown Life of Jesus Christ

posts.title: The Best Forgery Story of Modern Times (IMHO)
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Recounts how Konrad Kujau's fabricated Hitler diaries fooled prominent experts and publishers before forensic evidence and historical errors exposed the deception.
posts.searchSummary: Uses the Hitler diaries scandal to introduce the broader problem of modern literary forgery and purported discoveries. Describes how Konrad Kujau manufactured convincing notebooks, supplied a plausible provenance, and received millions before paper, ink, glue, and historical errors revealed the fraud. Follows the irony of Kujau's later career selling acknowledged imitations, which others then counterfeited, and an autobiography published under his name that he denied writing.

posts.title: Did Mark Make Up the Idea Jesus Was a Carpenter?
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Proposes that Mark's identification of Jesus as a carpenter reinforces his narrative of widespread misunderstanding about Jesus' identity as the suffering messiah.
posts.searchSummary: Suggests a literary reason for Mark 6:3 calling Jesus a carpenter, while leaving the historical question unresolved. Traces Mark's repeated failures of recognition among Jesus' family, neighbors, and disciples, culminating in the centurion's recognition after the crucifixion. Argues that the low status of a manual laborer could sharpen this motif, and considers Justin Martyr's later treatment of Jesus' carpentry as possible support for the interpretation.

posts.title: Casting Doubt on Jesus as the Carpenter…
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Questions whether Jesus was a carpenter, contrasting the limited textual evidence and rural working conditions with the absence of carpentry parables.
posts.searchSummary: Reexamines the assumption that Jesus worked as a carpenter, noting its dependence on Mark and the likely combination of farming with occasional craft work in Nazareth. Considers the demanding practical work of an ancient village carpenter and compares that background with Jesus' surviving parables. Observes that many concern money or agriculture but none clearly concern carpentry, presenting this as suggestive uncertainty rather than proof against the tradition.

posts.title: What’s Wrong with Being a Carpenter??
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Explores whether ancient disdain for manual labor explains why Gospel writers and later scribes changed Mark's identification of Jesus as a carpenter.
posts.searchSummary: Places Jesus' possible carpentry in the poor agricultural setting of Nazareth rather than the modern image of a respected craftsman. Uses Cicero's contempt for manual work and Celsus's criticism of Jesus' social standing to explain why the label could trouble educated Christians. Examines Origen's denial that the Gospels call Jesus a carpenter and proposes that similar concerns shaped changes by Matthew, Luke, and later scribes.

posts.title: Next Platinum Lecture on November 14th
posts.author: jennao
posts.description: Announces a November 14 Platinum member lecture on Nazareth, with live questions and a recording available afterward for members unable to attend.
posts.searchSummary: Announces the next quarterly Platinum member lecture, scheduled for November 14 at 2 p.m. Eastern, on what is known about Nazareth and the world into which Jesus was born. Describes the opportunity to ask Bart questions after the presentation and the availability of a recording for those unable to attend. Provides event logistics rather than the lecture's historical content, making this an administrative announcement.

posts.title: Was Jesus a Carpenter?  The Surprisingly Thin Evidence.
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Shows that identifying Jesus as a carpenter depends on Mark 6:3, whose wording other Gospel writers and later scribes altered.
posts.searchSummary: Reviews the unusually thin evidence for Jesus' occupation, locating the direct claim that he was a carpenter only in Mark 6:3. Compares Matthew's carpenter's son and Luke's son of Joseph, then examines later manuscripts that harmonize Mark with Matthew. Explains why textual scholars favor Mark's original wording while raising questions about the motives for changing it and the historical certainty of the occupational tradition.

posts.title: Supernatural “History.” Church Fathers. Atonement. Gospel Sources.  All Sorts of Questions!
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Explains historians' limits regarding miracles, patristic evidence for textual reconstruction, early atonement beliefs, and methods for identifying Mark's sources and themes.
posts.searchSummary: Answers four reader questions about historical method, textual evidence, atonement, and Gospel composition. Explains why divine intervention is outside historians' analytical reach and how church fathers' quotations reveal the wording of manuscripts from particular times and places. Relates early atonement beliefs to resurrection faith, then uses Mark's themes to assess whether apparent tensions reflect inherited sources, deliberate composition, or compatible teachings rather than demonstrable contradictions.

posts.title: An Even Stranger View of Eternity in the Book of Revelation
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Questions how Revelation's perfected world can still contain outside nations, sinners, and rulers after the apparent destruction of all God's enemies.
posts.searchSummary: Examines tensions between Revelation's destruction of God's enemies and its final portrayal of the New Jerusalem. Highlights references to other nations, kings, excluded sinners, and healing after the narrative has apparently eliminated death, suffering, and opposition to God. Asks whom the saints would rule in such a world and whether its imagery really implies a completely perfected eternity, leaving the interpretive problem open for discussion.

posts.title: The Irony of Jesus as the King of the Coming Kingdom
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Questions why Jesus and his disciples would need to govern a perfected kingdom, exploring tensions between heavenly equality, rewards, and rulership.
posts.searchSummary: Explores whether Jesus envisioned the coming earthly kingdom as completely free of inequality, wrongdoing, and the need for government. Considers alternative readings of his statement about marriage after the resurrection and his promise that the Twelve would rule Israel. Asks why kings and judges would be needed in a perfected world, treating these sayings as unresolved clues about differentiated rewards and possible hierarchy in the age to come.

posts.title: A Head-Scratcher in the Sermon on the Mount: Who Gets Into the Kingdom?
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Interprets Matthew's demanding teaching on Torah observance as allowing unequal rewards within God's kingdom, despite apparently conflicting statements about entry.
posts.searchSummary: Examines the tension in Matthew 5:17-20 between being least in the kingdom and needing righteousness greater than the scribes and Pharisees merely to enter. Reads Matthew's emphasis on obeying the law's deeper intent alongside criticism of hypocrisy and legal avoidance. Proposes that persistent disregard excludes people, while occasional violations permit entry with lesser rewards, making differentiated status rather than complete equality central to the passage.

posts.title: November 2026 Gold Q&A
posts.author: jennao
posts.description: Invites Gold and Platinum members to a November question-and-answer session, explaining advance submissions, live participation, and access to the recording.
posts.searchSummary: Announces a November 7 live question-and-answer session for Gold and Platinum members, with advance questions requested by November 5. Explains that the first half will address submitted questions and the second will allow participants to ask brief questions aloud. Provides joining instructions and promises a recording afterward, but contains no actual answers or substantive discussion of biblical subjects, so it is an administrative event notice.

posts.title: How Much Reward Do You Want?  The Tiers of Heaven
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Explains how the Apocalypse of Paul assigns unequal heavenly rewards and graded punishments reflecting the moral and theological concerns of later Christianity.
posts.searchSummary: Describes the Apocalypse of Paul's sharply differentiated afterlife, contrasting it with the earlier Apocalypse of Peter and relating its priorities to a Christianized empire. Surveys punishments directed at sinful believers, church leaders, and heretics, then follows progressively greater blessings for the righteous, sexually abstinent, and fully repentant. Shows that salvation does not imply equal glory in this influential tradition, introducing a later inquiry into Jesus' own expectations.

posts.title: Are People Treated Equally in the Age to Come?
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Reconsiders assumptions about equal heavenly rewards by introducing contrasting afterlife traditions in the Apocalypse of Peter and the Apocalypse of Paul.
posts.searchSummary: Distinguishes equal opportunity for salvation from equal experiences in the world to come, questioning an assumption often projected onto Jesus. Introduces the Apocalypse of Paul's dependence on the earlier Apocalypse of Peter, whose varied punishments contrast with the shared glory of the blessed. Sets up a comparison with later differentiated rewards while postponing the detailed analysis of Paul and the question of Jesus' own position.

posts.title: Great News For the Blog!  A Significant Milestone
posts.author: BDEhrman
posts.description: Reports a record fundraising milestone and explains how turning the New Testament blog series into a trade book supports charitable donations.
posts.searchSummary: Reports that the blog distributed $429,000 to charities through September and explains how a publishing advance helped reach that milestone. Describes transforming the New Testament in a Nutshell series from posts into an ebook and then a planned Norton trade book, with its advance directed to the Bart Ehrman Foundation. Connects this publishing arrangement with membership revenue, private donations, and the blog's wider charitable purpose.
